entries.real_world_scenario: It's difficult to imagine a child suffering any lasting negative effects on his/her psyche as a result of having been told any of these lies. But lying to children by omitting crucial information, such as the fact that he or she was adopted, can have grave emotional consequences. Sometimes what you perceive as a "little white lie," like shaving a few years off your age, may be considered a pretty big lie by someone else.
entries.case_study_cloze: Lying to a child about the tooth fairy leaving money under her pillow so that she won't feel so bad losing a tooth; lying to a child that there is a ____ so that he can enjoy the spirit and excitement of Christmas; or telling a child a partial truth about where babies come from, because she is too young to understand-all of these lies are part of modern American culture.

entries.real_world_scenario: In some cultures it is permissible to look at someone for three to four seconds, while in others anything beyond two seconds is considered rude. For instance, many African American and Hispanic children are taught to look down when addressed by elders, as a form of respect. In prison, for example, inmates will avoid eye contact with jailers or inmates known to be aggressive. Eye contact from high social status individuals, movie stars, for instance, makes us feel favored.

chimpanzees, as are our tribal instincts, which cause us to divide people
into insiders or outsiders.

entries.real_world_scenario: For example: Can a Darwinian understanding of human nature help people reach their goals in life? That is, does knowing how evolution has shaped our basic moral impulses help us decide which impulses we should consider legitimate? If you do, you're committing what philosophers call "the naturalistic fallacy" - the unwarranted inference of "ought" from "is." I agree: nature isn't a moral authority, and we needn't adopt any "values" that seem implicit in its workings - such as "might makes right."
entries.case_study_cloze: If you do, you're committing what philosophers call "the ____" - the unwarranted inference of "ought" from "is." I agree: nature isn't a moral authority, and we needn't adopt any "values" that seem implicit in its workings - such as "might makes right." Still, a true understanding of human nature will inevitably affect moral thought deeply and, as I will try to show, legitimately.
